headline: Earliest strong evidence for reef-like stromatolites
significance: Layered microbial structures in the Pilbara record show that communities were building persistent carbonate structures very early in Earth history.
why_it_matters: Establishes the deep biological ancestry of reef construction.

source_2_title: Grotzinger & Knoll (1999), Stromatolites in Precambrian carbonates
basic_headline: The oldest clear signs of reef like stromatolites
basic_significance: Stromatolites are layered structures built by communities of tiny microbes. Rocks from the Pilbara show that such communities were building long lasting carbonate structures very early in Earth's history.
basic_why: It shows that reef building goes back very deep into the history of life.

headline: Proterozoic microbial reefs become widespread
significance: Stromatolite and microbialite systems dominate many shallow carbonate platforms before animal reef builders become important.
why_it_matters: Provides the long pre-coral history of reef ecosystems.
source_1_title: Grotzinger & Knoll (1999), Stromatolites in Precambrian carbonates
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Reefs built by microbes become widespread
basic_significance: Reef systems built by microbes were the main structures on many shallow carbonate platforms. This was before animal reef builders became important.
basic_why: It gives reef ecosystems a long history from before corals existed.

headline: First metazoan framework reefs
significance: Cloudina–Namacalathus and modular Namapoikia communities formed rigid frameworks near the end of the Ediacaran.
why_it_matters: Marks the transition from purely microbial to animal-supported reefs.

source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: The first reefs with frameworks built by animals
basic_significance: Near the end of the Ediacaran, communities of early animals called Cloudina, Namacalathus and Namapoikia built rigid frameworks.
basic_why: It marks the change from reefs made only by microbes to reefs held up by animals.

basic_why: It was the first big spread of reefs built by animals.

significance: Archaeocyath reef building collapses during Early–Middle Cambrian environmental turnover.

basic_significance: Reef building by archaeocyaths collapsed as the environment changed between the Early and Middle Cambrian.

headline: Ordovician reef expansion begins

source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs

basic_significance: Stromatoporoid sponges, bryozoans and early corals all spread. This happened during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, a time when many new kinds of sea life appeared.
basic_why: Reefs became major places where new kinds of sea life appeared.

basic_headline: Tabulate and rugose corals become major parts of reefs
basic_significance: Coral groups of the Palaeozoic added more and more to reef frameworks. They built alongside sponges called stromatoporoids.
basic_why: It was the first big phase of reefs dominated by corals, although not by the modern stony corals called scleractinians.

headline: End-Ordovician mass extinction disrupts reefs
significance: Glaciation and rapid sea-level change cause one of the Big Five extinctions and major reef loss.
why_it_matters: First mass-extinction marker on the reef timeline.

source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: A mass extinction at the end of the Ordovician hits reefs
basic_significance: Growing ice and fast changes in sea level caused one of the Big Five mass extinctions. Reefs suffered major losses.
basic_why: It is the first mass extinction marked on the reef timeline.

headline: Silurian reef recovery
significance: Stromatoporoid–tabulate reef systems recover and spread across tropical shelves.
why_it_matters: Shows post-extinction rebuilding of reef ecosystems.

basic_headline: Reefs recover during the Silurian
basic_significance: Reef systems built by stromatoporoid sponges and tabulate corals recovered. They spread again across tropical shelves.
basic_why: It shows reef ecosystems rebuilding after a mass extinction.

headline: Devonian reef zenith
significance: Large stromatoporoid–coral reef complexes reach some of the greatest extents of the Palaeozoic.
why_it_matters: A high-water mark for pre-scleractinian reef building.
source_1_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Reef building reaches its peak in the Devonian
basic_significance: Large reef complexes built by stromatoporoid sponges and corals became some of the biggest of the whole Palaeozoic.
basic_why: It was a high point for reef building before the modern stony corals appeared.

headline: Late Devonian reef collapse
significance: Repeated anoxia, climate and sea-level perturbations eliminate most stromatoporoid–coral reef systems.
why_it_matters: One of the most severe and prolonged reef crises.
source_1_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
source_2_title: Dishon et al. (2020), Traits enabling scleractinian survival through mass extinctions
basic_headline: Reefs collapse in the Late Devonian
basic_significance: The sea lost its oxygen again and again, and the climate and sea level kept shifting. Most reef systems built by stromatoporoid sponges and corals were wiped out.
basic_why: It was one of the most severe and longest lasting reef crises.

headline: Early Carboniferous “reef gap”
significance: Large metazoan frameworks remain uncommon; microbial and algal mounds dominate many carbonate settings.
why_it_matters: Illustrates ecological replacement after a reef crisis.
source_1_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: A reef gap opens in the Early Carboniferous
basic_significance: Large reef frameworks built by animals stayed uncommon. Mounds built by microbes and algae were the main structures in many carbonate settings.
basic_why: It shows one kind of reef builder taking the place of another after a reef crisis.

headline: Late Carboniferous reef recovery remains patchy
significance: Sponges, algae and microbes form localized reef and mound systems under icehouse conditions.
why_it_matters: Reef recovery does not always recreate earlier ecosystems.
source_1_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Reef recovery stays patchy in the Late Carboniferous
basic_significance: Sponges, algae and microbes built reefs and mounds in scattered places. This happened in a cold icehouse climate.
basic_why: Reef recovery does not always rebuild the ecosystems that came before.

headline: Photosymbiosis may predate the fossil radiation
significance: Phylogenetic analyses infer an older scleractinian ancestry and photosymbiosis long before abundant Triassic fossils.
why_it_matters: Separates lineage origin from the first abundant skeletal record.
source_1_title: Vaga et al. (2025), A global coral phylogeny reveals resilience and vulnerability
source_2_title: Stolarski et al. (2011), Ancient evolutionary origins of Scleractinia
basic_headline: Corals may have partnered with algae earlier than the fossils show
basic_significance: Scientists studied coral family trees. This work suggests that stony corals, and photosymbiosis, their partnership with tiny algae living inside them, began long before the many Triassic fossils.
basic_why: It separates when the coral family line began from when their skeletons first became common as fossils.

headline: Permian sponge–algal reef expansion
significance: Diverse sponge, microbial and algal frameworks develop along tropical Pangaean margins.
why_it_matters: Last major reef systems before Earth’s largest mass extinction.
source_1_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Sponge and algal reefs expand in the Permian
basic_significance: Many different frameworks built by sponges, microbes and algae grew along the tropical edges of the supercontinent Pangaea.
basic_why: They were the last major reef systems before Earth's largest mass extinction.

headline: End-Permian mass extinction devastates reefs
significance: The largest Phanerozoic extinction removes Palaeozoic reef builders and collapses carbonate ecosystems.
why_it_matters: The most profound reset in reef history.
source_1_title: Brayard et al. (2011), Transient metazoan reefs after the end-Permian extinction
source_2_title: Dishon et al. (2020), Traits enabling scleractinian survival through mass extinctions
basic_headline: The end Permian mass extinction devastates reefs
basic_significance: This was the largest extinction of the Phanerozoic. It removed the reef builders of the Palaeozoic and collapsed the ecosystems that made carbonate rock.
basic_why: It was the deepest reset in the whole history of reefs.

headline: Microbial reefs dominate the immediate aftermath
significance: Microbialites flourish in stressed Early Triassic seas where complex metazoan reefs are largely absent.
why_it_matters: A classic post-extinction ecological simplification.
source_1_title: Brayard et al. (2011), Transient metazoan reefs after the end-Permian extinction
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Microbe built reefs take over straight afterwards
basic_significance: Microbialites, which are reefs built by microbes, thrived in the stressed seas of the Early Triassic. Complex reefs built by animals were mostly missing.
basic_why: It is a classic case of an ecosystem becoming much simpler after a mass extinction.

headline: Unexpectedly early post-Permian metazoan reefs
significance: Small sponge–bivalve reefs show that local complex communities returned sooner than once assumed.
why_it_matters: Revises the tempo of reef recovery.
source_1_title: Brayard et al. (2011), Transient metazoan reefs after the end-Permian extinction
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Animal reefs return sooner than expected after the Permian
basic_significance: Small reefs built by sponges and bivalve shellfish have been found. They show that complex communities came back in some places sooner than people once assumed.
basic_why: It changes our idea of how fast reefs can recover.

headline: Middle Triassic reef rebuilding accelerates
significance: Sponges, microbes and emerging scleractinians re-establish substantial frameworks.
why_it_matters: Sets the ecological stage for modern stony corals.
source_1_title: Stolarski et al. (2011), Ancient evolutionary origins of Scleractinia
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Reef rebuilding speeds up in the Middle Triassic
basic_significance: Sponges, microbes and the first scleractinians, which are stony corals, built large frameworks again.
basic_why: It set the scene for the modern stony corals.

headline: Scleractinian corals appear in the fossil record
significance: Modern-style aragonitic stony corals become recognizable in Middle Triassic deposits.
why_it_matters: Conventional fossil first appearance of the principal modern reef builders.
source_1_title: Shinzato et al. (2011), Acropora digitifera genome
source_2_title: Stolarski et al. (2011), Ancient evolutionary origins of Scleractinia
basic_headline: Stony corals appear in the fossil record
basic_significance: Stony corals of the modern kind can be recognised in Middle Triassic rocks. Their skeletons are made of a mineral called aragonite.
basic_why: These fossils are usually taken as the first appearance of the main reef builders of today.

headline: Triassic coral–sponge reefs spread
significance: Scleractinians diversify and form increasingly extensive reefs in warm Tethyan seas.
why_it_matters: First sustained expansion of modern coral-style reefs.
source_1_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
source_2_title: Stolarski et al. (2011), Ancient evolutionary origins of Scleractinia
basic_headline: Coral and sponge reefs spread through the Triassic
basic_significance: Stony corals split into more and more kinds and built larger reefs. This happened in the warm seas of the Tethys.
basic_why: It was the first lasting spread of reefs built in the modern coral style.

headline: End-Triassic extinction causes another reef crisis
significance: Volcanism, warming and ocean acidification sharply reduce reef building at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary.
why_it_matters: A major test of scleractinian persistence.

basic_headline: The end Triassic extinction causes another reef crisis
basic_significance: Volcanoes, warming and ocean acidification, which makes seawater more acidic, sharply cut reef building. This happened at the boundary between the Triassic and the Jurassic.
basic_why: It was a major test of whether stony corals could keep going.

significance: Scleractinian frameworks re-establish across warm epicontinental seas.
why_it_matters: Modern reef builders recover after the end-Triassic crisis.

source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Coral reefs recover and expand in the Jurassic
basic_significance: Stony corals built their frameworks again across warm seas that spread over the continents.
basic_why: The modern reef builders recovered after the end Triassic crisis.

headline: Rudist bivalves rival corals as reef builders
significance: In many Cretaceous seas, rudists replace corals as dominant framework constructors.
why_it_matters: Reef habitat persists even when corals are not dominant.
source_1_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Rudist shellfish rival corals as reef builders
basic_significance: Rudists were bivalves, shellfish with two shells. In many Cretaceous seas they took the place of corals as the main framework builders.
basic_why: Reef habitat can carry on even when corals are not the main builders.

headline: Ocean-anoxic events repeatedly reorganize reefs
significance: Greenhouse warming, anoxia and ocean chemistry shifts drive reef turnovers during the mid-Cretaceous.
why_it_matters: A deep-time analogue for multiple interacting stressors.
source_1_title: Quattrini et al. (2020), Palaeoclimate and ocean conditions shaped coral evolution
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Losses of ocean oxygen keep reorganising reefs
basic_significance: Greenhouse warming, loss of oxygen in the sea and changes in ocean chemistry kept changing which creatures built reefs. This happened through the middle of the Cretaceous.
basic_why: It is an example from deep time of several stresses acting together on reefs.

headline: Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction removes rudist reefs
significance: Rudist bivalves disappear and photosymbiotic shallow corals suffer disproportionate losses.
why_it_matters: Ends the last major non-coral reef-building regime.
source_1_title: Dishon et al. (2020), Traits enabling scleractinian survival through mass extinctions
source_2_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
basic_headline: The Cretaceous to Paleogene extinction removes rudist reefs
basic_significance: Rudist bivalves disappeared. Shallow corals that host tiny algae inside them suffered unusually heavy losses.
basic_why: It ended the last major time when reefs were built mainly by animals other than corals.

headline: Reef frameworks reappear after K–Pg
significance: Coralline algae, foraminifera and surviving corals rebuild patchy reef systems within a few million years.
why_it_matters: Rapid but compositionally novel recovery.
source_1_title: Dishon et al. (2020), Traits enabling scleractinian survival through mass extinctions
source_2_title: Kiessling (2009), Geologic and biologic controls on the evolution of reefs
basic_headline: Reef frameworks reappear after the Cretaceous Paleogene extinction
basic_significance: Coralline algae, small shelled creatures called foraminifera and the corals that survived rebuilt patchy reef systems. This took a few million years.
basic_why: The recovery was fast, but the reefs were made up of a new mix of life.

headline: Eocene greenhouse reefs diversify
significance: Modern coral families and large benthic foraminifera expand during warm Eocene climates.
why_it_matters: Builds much of the modern coral evolutionary stock.
source_1_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
source_2_title: Quattrini et al. (2020), Palaeoclimate and ocean conditions shaped coral evolution
basic_headline: Eocene greenhouse reefs become more varied
basic_significance: Modern coral families spread during the warm climates of the Eocene. Large foraminifera living on the sea floor spread as well.
basic_why: It built much of the coral family stock we still have today.

headline: Eocene–Oligocene cooling triggers coral turnover
significance: Rapid global cooling and ice-sheet growth coincide with a marked extinction pulse in reef corals.
why_it_matters: Shows that cooling as well as warming can restructure reefs.
source_1_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
source_2_title: Quattrini et al. (2020), Palaeoclimate and ocean conditions shaped coral evolution
basic_headline: Cooling after the Eocene brings a coral turnover
basic_significance: The world cooled quickly and ice sheets grew. At the same time, reef corals went through a clear pulse of extinction.
basic_why: It shows that cooling, as well as warming, can reshape reefs.

headline: Miocene reef-coral radiation
significance: Coral diversity and reef building expand across the Tethys and Indo-West Pacific.
why_it_matters: Creates many lineages central to modern reefs.
source_1_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Reef corals spread and diversify in the Miocene
basic_significance: Coral diversity grew and reef building expanded. This spread across the Tethys and the Indo-West Pacific.
basic_why: It created many coral lines that are central to reefs today.

headline: Coral diversity shifts toward the Indo-Pacific
significance: Tethyan closure and tectonic reorganization concentrate coral diversity in the developing Coral Triangle.
why_it_matters: Explains the modern centre of coral biodiversity.
source_1_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
source_2_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
basic_headline: Coral variety shifts towards the Indo-Pacific
basic_significance: The old Tethys seaway closed and the Earth's plates shifted position. This gathered the greatest variety of corals into the growing Coral Triangle.
basic_why: It explains where the centre of coral variety sits today.

headline: Isthmus of Panama separates Atlantic and Pacific reefs
significance: Final closure reorganizes currents, nutrients and evolutionary trajectories on both sides of the Americas.
why_it_matters: Creates two contrasting modern reef provinces.
source_1_title: Kiessling et al. (2010), Reefs as cradles of evolution and sources of biodiversity
source_2_title: Siqueira et al. (2022), Fast-growing species shape reef-coral evolution
basic_headline: The Isthmus of Panama splits Atlantic and Pacific reefs
basic_significance: The narrow strip of land at Panama finally closed the gap between the two oceans. This changed currents, nutrients and the way life evolved on both sides of the Americas.
basic_why: It created two modern reef regions that are very different from each other.

headline: Acroporid diversification accelerates

why_it_matters: Helps explain the ecological prominence—and vulnerability—of modern Acropora.

source_2_title: Royal Society (1898), The Atoll of Funafuti: borings into a coral reef

basic_significance: Scientists drilled deep holes at Bikini and Enewetak. They passed through more than a kilometre of coral limestone before they reached the volcanic rock underneath.
basic_why: It was the strongest direct test yet, and it backed up Darwin's idea that the volcanoes slowly sank.

headline: Whole-reef metabolism is quantified
significance: Odum and Odum measure production and respiration on Enewetak, framing reefs as high-throughput ecosystems.
why_it_matters: Introduces ecosystem energetics to reef science.
source_1_title: Odum & Odum (1955), Trophic structure and productivity of a windward coral reef
source_2_title: Johannes et al. (1972), The metabolism of some coral reef communities
basic_headline: Scientists measured the energy used by a whole reef
basic_significance: Odum and Odum measured how much food a reef made and how much it used up, at Enewetak. They described reefs as places where energy moves through very fast.
basic_why: It brought the study of energy flow into reef science.

headline: Photosynthesis is shown to accelerate coral calcification
significance: Goreau experimentally links light and algal photosynthesis to skeletal deposition.
why_it_matters: Mechanistically connects symbiosis to reef building.

basic_headline: Light was shown to help corals build their skeletons faster
basic_significance: Goreau ran experiments that linked light, and the food made by the tiny algae living in the coral, to how fast the coral built its skeleton.
basic_why: It showed how the partnership between a coral and its algae helps build reefs.

significance: Dense Acanthaster populations are observed near Green Island and later spread, initiating a major ecological and management debate.
why_it_matters: Introduces a recurrent biological driver of coral loss.
source_1_title: Australian Institute of Marine Science, Understanding crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks
source_2_title: De’ath et al. (2012), The 27-year decline of coral cover on the Great Barrier Reef

basic_headline: First crown of thorns outbreaks of modern times recorded on the Great Barrier Reef
basic_significance: Large numbers of crown of thorns starfish were seen near Green Island, and later spread further. This started a major argument among scientists and reef managers.
basic_why: It brought in a living cause of coral loss that keeps coming back.

headline: Aquanaut programmes extend direct reef observation
significance: Saturation diving and underwater habitats allow longer-duration behavioural and ecological research on reefs.
why_it_matters: Expands observation time below the surface.
source_1_title: HMS Challenger expedition preliminary account (1876)
source_2_title: Global Reef Record / XL Catlin Seaview Survey archive

basic_headline: Divers staying underwater could study reefs for longer
basic_significance: Saturation diving and underwater living stations let scientists stay below the surface for longer. They could study reef life and animal behaviour for longer stretches.
basic_why: It gave scientists more time to watch reefs below the surface.

headline: Carbon transfer from zooxanthellae to coral is demonstrated
significance: Radiotracer experiments show that algal photosynthate supplies a major share of coral metabolism.
why_it_matters: Explains how reefs thrive in nutrient-poor tropical waters.
source_1_title: Muscatine & Cernichiari (1969), Assimilation of photosynthetic products by reef corals
source_2_title: Goreau (1959), Physiology of skeleton formation in corals I
basic_headline: Tiny algae inside corals were shown to feed them
basic_significance: Experiments using traceable carbon showed that food made by the algae inside a coral supplies a large share of what the coral needs to live.
basic_why: It helps explain how reefs do so well in tropical water that holds few nutrients.

headline: Reef community metabolism and nutrient recycling are quantified
significance: Community-scale studies show tight recycling and high productivity despite low surrounding nutrients.
why_it_matters: Establishes the “oasis in an ocean desert” mechanism.
source_1_title: Johannes et al. (1972), The metabolism of some coral reef communities
source_2_title: Odum & Odum (1955), Trophic structure and productivity of a windward coral reef
basic_headline: Reefs were shown to recycle nutrients very tightly
basic_significance: Studies of whole reef communities showed that reefs use the same nutrients over and over. They produce a lot of life even though the water around them has few nutrients.
basic_why: It explained how a reef can be an oasis in an ocean desert.

headline: Bacteria are recognized as important reef trophic components
significance: Microbial production and consumption become explicit parts of coral-reef food-web models.
why_it_matters: Begins the modern view of reefs as microbial as well as coral ecosystems.
source_1_title: Sorokin (1973), Trophical role of bacteria in coral reef communities
source_2_title: Rohwer et al. (2002), Diversity and distribution of coral-associated bacteria
basic_headline: Bacteria were recognised as an important part of reef food webs
basic_significance: Scientists began putting microbes into their models of reef food webs. What these tiny living things make, and what they eat, became part of the picture.
basic_why: It started the modern view that reefs are made of microbes as well as corals.

headline: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act creates a vast management framework
significance: Australia establishes the statutory basis for managing most of the GBR as a multiple-use marine park.
why_it_matters: A landmark in large-scale reef governance.
source_1_title: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975
source_2_title: UNESCO World Heritage Committee, Great Barrier Reef inscription (1981)
basic_headline: A new Australian law created the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park
basic_significance: Australia passed a law to manage most of the Great Barrier Reef as a marine park. The park was set up to allow several different uses of the area.
basic_why: It was a landmark in looking after a reef on a very large scale.

headline: Intermediate-disturbance theory places reefs at the centre of ecological debate
significance: Connell uses coral reefs and rainforests to argue that disturbance can maintain high diversity.
why_it_matters: Connects reef dynamics to general ecological theory.

source_2_title: Graham et al. (2015), Predicting climate-driven regime shifts versus rebound potential
basic_headline: A new idea said some disturbance can keep reefs rich in species
basic_significance: Connell used coral reefs and rainforests to argue that damage and disturbance can keep the number of species high.
basic_why: It connected the way reefs work to wider ideas in ecology.

headline: Modern mass-bleaching observations enter the scientific record
significance: Widespread paling associated with anomalous heat is documented at multiple tropical locations.
why_it_matters: Marks the beginning of the modern mass-bleaching era.

source_2_title: Glynn (1984), Widespread coral mortality and the 1982–83 El Niño
basic_headline: Modern mass bleaching entered the scientific record
basic_significance: Scientists recorded corals turning pale, which is called bleaching, over wide areas at several tropical places. The paling happened alongside unusually warm water.
basic_why: It marks the start of the modern time of mass bleaching.

basic_headline: Bonaire protected the water around its whole island
basic_significance: The sea around Bonaire and Klein Bonaire was made a protected park. It became an early model for looking after reefs and running diving tourism.
basic_why: It was an early piece of official reef protection outside Australia.

significance: UNESCO recognizes the reef’s global natural values and geological–ecological significance.
why_it_matters: Adds international oversight and a durable conservation benchmark.

source_2_title: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975
basic_headline: The Great Barrier Reef was listed as World Heritage
basic_significance: UNESCO recognised that the reef matters to the whole world. It listed the reef as important for both its rocks and its living things.
basic_why: It added international oversight and set a lasting standard for protecting the reef.

significance: Field observations on the GBR reveal mass annual release of eggs and sperm by many coral species.

basic_significance: Scientists watching the Great Barrier Reef saw many coral species release their eggs and sperm at the same time. It happens as one big event once a year.
basic_why: It changed what we know about how corals breed, how reefs are linked, and when to do repair work.

basic_significance: Heat stress killed a large share of the corals around Panama, the Galápagos and nearby reefs.

source_2_title: Mumby et al. (2006), Fishing, trophic cascades, and herbivory on coral reefs

basic_significance: A disease spread through the water and killed Diadema, the sea urchin that ate most of the algae. With the urchins gone, algae spread on many reefs.
basic_why: It worked like a huge natural experiment across the whole region, showing what happens when grazers are lost and a reef changes state.

significance: Scleractinia are listed under CITES Appendix II, requiring permits for international trade.

basic_why: It treated coral collecting, and the aquarium and ornament trade, as issues for countries to handle together.

basic_headline: Replanting one coral could help a reef match 0.5 m of sea level rise
basic_significance: At Buck Island Reef, replanting elkhorn coral is projected to turn around the reef's wearing away. It could then match the sea level rise expected by 2100 if emissions are cut moderately.
basic_why: It is a rare projection where action changes the outcome. The condition attached is that it works alongside emissions cuts, not instead of them.

headline: Reef carbonate production can recover this century, but only with strong mitigation
significance: A coral module embedded inside a carbon-climate model. Without thermal adaptation, production falls below a quarter of historical values. With adaptation and high mitigation, it recovers to 50–90%.
why_it_matters: Shows how much of the projected range comes from a single uncertain biological assumption: whether corals can raise their bleaching thresholds.
source_1_title: Bouttes et al. (2025), Projections of coral reef carbonate production from a global climate–coral reef coupled model
editorial_notes: Projection. Placed at its stated projection year; see proj_* columns.
proj_scenario: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways; high-emission vs high-mitigation
proj_quote: We show that without thermal adaptation, global coral reef carbonate production decreases to less than 25 % of historical values in most scenarios over the 21st century, with limited further declines between 2100 and 2300 irrespective of the climate sensitivity.
basic_headline: Reefs could build stone again this century but only with strong emissions cuts
basic_significance: Researchers put a coral model inside a climate and carbon model. Without corals adapting to heat, reef building falls below a quarter of its past levels. With adaptation and strong emissions cuts, it recovers to between 50 and 90%.
basic_why: It shows how much of the range in these projections comes from one uncertain question about biology. That question is whether corals can raise the temperature at which they bleach.

headline: A bleaching rate above 7.9% a year tips reefs into lasting degradation
significance: A data-driven model fitted to historical field observations identifies a threshold annual bleaching rate, and finds it exceeded across all major tropical regions by the end of the century even under optimistic mitigation.
why_it_matters: Puts a number on the point where repeated bleaching stops being a series of events and becomes a change of state.
source_1_title: Zeng et al. (2025), Inevitable global coral reef decline under climate change-induced thermal stresses
editorial_notes: Projection. Placed at its stated projection year; see proj_* columns.
proj_scenario: multiple emission scenarios, including optimistic mitigation
proj_quote: Alarmingly, even under the most optimistic mitigation pathways, substantial degradation is projected across all major tropical marine regions by the end of the century.
basic_headline: Bleaching above 7.9% a year could tip reefs into lasting damage
basic_significance: A model built from real field observations found a tipping point in the yearly bleaching rate. It finds that rate passed across every major tropical region by the end of the century, even with hopeful emissions cuts.
basic_why: It puts a number on the point where repeated bleaching stops being a run of separate events. Past that point the reef has changed state.

headline: IPCC: reefs decline a further 70–90% at 1.5°C, and more than 99% at 2°C
significance: The single most quoted number about the future of coral reefs, from the Special Report on 1.5°C. It is stated against warming levels, not against years.
why_it_matters: The half-degree between the two Paris targets is, for reefs, close to the difference between a remnant and none.
source_1_title: IPCC (2018), Global Warming of 1.5°C, Chapter 3: Impacts of 1.5°C Global Warming on Natural and Human Systems
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: Coral reefs, for example, are projected to decline by a further 70–90% at 1.5°C (high confidence) with larger losses (>99%) at 2ºC (very high confidence).
proj_quote_note: IPCC SR1.5, Summary for Policymakers, paragraph B.4.2, which cites Chapter 3 section 3.4.4 and Box 3.4.

headline: Keeping more than a tenth of reefs needs warming held below 1.5°C
significance: An early comprehensive treatment of bleaching in terms of global mean temperature. Even under the most optimistic scenario assessed, and generous assumptions about adaptation, a third of reefs are projected to degrade over the long term.
why_it_matters: Set the framing that reef outcomes should be stated against warming levels rather than dates, which most later work followed.
source_1_title: Frieler et al. (2012), Limiting global warming to 2 °C is unlikely to save most coral reefs
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: We show that preserving >10% of coral reefs worldwide would require limiting warming to below 1.5 °C (atmosphere–ocean general circulation models (AOGCMs) range: 1.3–1.8 °C) relative to pre-industrial levels.
basic_headline: Saving more than a tenth of reefs needs warming kept below 1.5°C
basic_significance: This was an early full study of bleaching described in terms of global average temperature. Even under the most hopeful scenario it looked at, and with generous assumptions about corals adapting, a third of reefs are projected to decline over the long term.
basic_why: It set the habit of describing reef outcomes against warming levels rather than dates. Most later work followed it.

headline: Local thermal refuges all but vanish at 1.5°C, and completely at 2°C
significance: At 1 km resolution across more than 230,000 reef pixels, the share of reef acting as a thermal refuge falls from 84% today to 0.2% at 1.5°C and zero at 2°C. Upwelling and strong currents rarely help.
why_it_matters: Undercuts the strategy of protecting the coolest reefs and hoping they carry the rest, which had been a central plank of climate-smart reef management.
source_1_title: Dixon et al. (2022), Future loss of local-scale thermal refugia in coral reef ecosystems
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: Here, we show that climate change will overwhelm current local-scale refugia, with declines in global thermal refugia from 84% of global coral reef pixels in the present-day climate to 0.2% at 1.5°C, and 0% at 2.0°C of global warming.
basic_headline: Cool refuges for reefs nearly vanish at 1.5°C and are gone at 2°C
basic_significance: The study covered more than 230,000 reef squares of about one kilometre each. The share of reef acting as a cool refuge from heat falls from 84% today to 0.2% at 1.5°C, and to zero at 2°C. Cold water rising from below and strong currents rarely help.
basic_why: It weakens the plan of protecting the coolest reefs and hoping they carry the rest. That plan had been a central part of climate smart reef management.

headline: Great Barrier Reef refuges hold their advantage only until about 3°C
significance: The reefs that escaped the worst thermal stress over the past twenty years did so because of tides and wind mixing warm water away from the surface. That physical advantage survives warming, up to a point.
why_it_matters: A more hopeful reading of refuges than the global picture, with a hard ceiling attached.
source_1_title: McWhorter et al. (2022), Climate refugia on the Great Barrier Reef fail when global warming exceeds 3°C
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: However, on average this relative advantage only persists until global warming exceeds ~3°C.
basic_headline: Great Barrier Reef cool refuges keep their advantage only to about 3°C
basic_significance: Some reefs escaped the worst heat stress over the past twenty years. Tides and wind mixed warm water away from the surface there. That physical advantage survives warming, but only up to a point.
basic_why: It is a more hopeful view of refuges than the global picture, with a hard ceiling attached.

headline: Corals can evolve fast enough to survive, but only on low-emissions pathways
significance: Genomic simulations for a cool-water population in the Cook Islands show heat tolerance evolving fast enough for the population to persist under RCP2.6 and RCP4.5, and not fast enough under RCP6.0 or RCP8.5.
why_it_matters: Puts a boundary on natural adaptation: it is real, it is measurable, and it is outpaced above a certain rate of warming.
source_1_title: Bay et al. (2017), Genomic models predict successful coral adaptation if future ocean warming rates are reduced
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_scenario: RCP2.6 and RCP4.5 (persistence) vs RCP6.0 and RCP8.5 (extinction)
proj_quote: Under more severe scenarios, RCP6.0 and RCP8.5, adaptation was not rapid enough to prevent extinction.
basic_headline: Corals could evolve fast enough to survive but only with low emissions
basic_significance: Computer models of genes looked at a cool water coral population in the Cook Islands. Heat tolerance evolves fast enough for the population to keep going under RCP2.6 and RCP4.5. It is not fast enough under RCP6.0 or RCP8.5.
basic_why: It puts a boundary on natural adaptation. Adaptation is real and can be measured, but it is outpaced above a certain speed of warming.

headline: Enough genetic variation exists for region-wide adaptation over 100–250 years
significance: Population genomics plus larval dispersal modelling for Acropora millepora finds southward migration spreading heat-tolerant alleles, and standing variation sufficient to adapt to gradual warming. The same model predicts rising sensitivity to sudden heatwaves.
why_it_matters: The most optimistic adaptation projection here, and it comes with the caveat that gradual warming and marine heatwaves are different problems.
source_1_title: Matz et al. (2018), Potential and limits for rapid genetic adaptation to warming in a Great Barrier Reef coral
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: Despite this capacity for adaptation, our model predicts that coral populations would become increasingly sensitive to random thermal fluctuations such as ENSO cycles or heat waves, which corresponds well with the recent increase in frequency of catastrophic coral bleaching events.
basic_headline: Corals across one region could hold enough genetic variety to adapt over 100 to 250 years
basic_significance: Scientists studied the genes of Acropora millepora and modelled how its young drift on currents. Young corals drifting south spread heat tolerant gene versions, and the genetic variety already there is enough to adapt to gradual warming. The same model predicts corals becoming more sensitive to sudden heatwaves.
basic_why: It is the most hopeful adaptation projection here. It comes with the warning that gradual warming and marine heatwaves are different problems.

headline: Large-scale intervention buys the Great Barrier Reef one to two decades
significance: A meta-community model of 3,753 reefs tests combinations of crown-of-thorns control, rubble stabilisation, water quality measures, solar radiation management and heat-tolerant corals. None avert decline; the strongest combinations delay it.
why_it_matters: The clearest statement of what reef intervention is for. It is a way of buying time for mitigation to work, not a substitute for it.
source_1_title: Condie et al. (2021), Large-scale interventions may delay decline of the Great Barrier Reef
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: Without intervention, all climate scenarios resulted in precipitous declines in GBR coral cover over the next 50 years.
basic_headline: Big rescue efforts could buy the Great Barrier Reef ten to twenty years
basic_significance: A model of 3,753 connected reefs tested mixes of crown of thorns control, holding loose rubble in place, better water quality, reflecting some sunlight away and heat tolerant corals. None of the mixes stop the decline. The strongest ones only delay it.
basic_why: It is the clearest statement of what reef intervention is for. It is a way of buying time for emissions cuts to work, not a replacement for them.

headline: Swapping algal partners delays decline, until the warming rate outruns it
significance: A global model of competing coral growth forms finds symbiont shuffling towards heat-tolerant types more effective than symbiont evolution, and both overtaken under high emissions. Acidification matters far less than warming.
why_it_matters: Vulnerability depends on the interaction between how fast it warms and how fast corals can respond, so neither warming nor adaptive capacity predicts the outcome on its own.
source_1_title: Logan et al. (2021), Quantifying global potential for coral evolutionary response to climate change
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: We show symbiont shuffling (towards taxa with increased heat tolerance) was more effective than symbiont evolution in delaying coral-cover declines, but stronger warming rates (high emissions scenarios) outpace the ability of these adaptive processes and limit coral persistence.
basic_headline: Swapping algae partners delays decline until warming gets too fast
basic_significance: A global model of competing coral growth forms looked at the tiny algae living inside corals. Corals shuffling towards heat tolerant algae types works better than those algae evolving, and under high emissions both are overtaken. The sea turning more acidic matters far less than warming.
basic_why: How badly reefs suffer depends on how fast it warms and how fast corals can respond together. So neither warming nor the ability to adapt predicts the outcome on its own.

headline: Transplanting heat-tolerant corals helps only if sustained for a century
significance: An eco-evolutionary simulation of restoration and assisted evolution finds both have a limited effect on severe decline, and that building genetic variance may outperform introducing heat-tolerant genotypes.
why_it_matters: A direct test of the assumption behind much reef restoration, and the answer is that scale and duration matter more than the choice of coral.
source_1_title: DeFilippo et al. (2022), Assessing the potential for demographic restoration and assisted evolution to build climate resilience in coral reefs
editorial_notes: Projection stated against a warming level or emissions scenario, not a date. Corridor position implies no timing.
proj_quote: Overall, we found that, although demographic restoration and assisted evolution have the potential to improve long‐term coral cover, both approaches had a limited impact in preventing severe declines under climate change scenarios.
basic_headline: Planting heat tolerant corals helps only if kept up for a century
basic_significance: A computer model followed replanting corals and helping them evolve, along with how coral genes change over time. Both have only a limited effect on severe decline. Building up genetic variety may work better than adding corals with heat tolerant genes.
basic_why: It is a direct test of the idea behind much reef restoration. The answer is that scale and how long it lasts matter more than which coral is chosen.
